Title: MicroAdapt : Self-Evolutionary Dynamic Modeling Algorithms for Time-evolving Data Streams

for Time-evolving Data Streams

Abstract
Recently, we have been inundated with dynamic, time-evolving
activity data streams generated by various individual IoT/sensor de-
vices (e.g., healthcare devices and factory equipment). What would
be the ideal mechanism for adaptively summarizing and modeling
individual and local activities directly on small IoT devices with lim-
ited computing resources? In this paper, we present MicroAdapt,
which comprises scalable and effective algorithms for modeling
and forecasting time-evolving data streams. Our proposed method
has the following advantages: (a) Adaptivity: it continuously mon-
itors the latest time-series patterns in data streams, recognizes
any sudden changes, updates model parameters, and enables real-
time, long-range forecasting; (b) Any-time processing: it operates
on a large collection of data streams, requiring a constant time (i.e.,
𝑂(1)) for model updates and future predictions, at any point in time;
(c) Lightweight computing: it does not require high-performance
computing machines equipped with powerful GPUs, such as those
used in deep learning, and can run on lightweight computers or
even “edge” computing devices, such as Raspberry Pi. Intuitively,
our method is inspired by the concept of an evolutionary adapta-
tion mechanism of microorganisms, and thus it enables adaptive,
any-time, lightweight model estimation and summarization of non-
stationary data streams whose time-series patterns are constantly
changing over time. We conduct extensive experiments on real
datasets and demonstrate that MicroAdapt effectively captures im-
portant time-series patterns in the data streams, makes long-range
forecasts, and consistently outperforms the existing state-of-the-art
methods (e.g., TSMixer) as regards accuracy and execution speed.
MicroAdapt improves accuracy by about 60% for MSE and 30%
for MAE, while reducing computation time by up to six orders of
magnitude (more than 100,000 times). We also applied our ana-
lytics to experiments implemented on Raspberry Pi with real IoT
data streams, thus demonstrating the practicality and effectiveness
of our approach. In fact, our proposed method required less than
1.95GB of memory and consumed less than 1.69W of power.

Introduction
In recent years, with the rapid spread of IoT devices in various
fields, such as healthcare and industry, there has been a growing
demand to analyze large numbers of complex data streams collected
from individual/personal devices at high speed, and utilize them
for advanced services. For example, for wearable devices and em-
bedded systems used in healthcare services [23], or manufacturing
[47], we need to extract important patterns quickly and effectively
to enable us to predict users’ subsequent conditions or potential
problems immediately on small and personalized devices with lim-
ited computing resources. In addition, the privacy/confidentiality of
the measured data should be carefully considered; ideally, the data
should be analyzed securely in local (i.e., “edge”) devices without
directly sending raw data to the cloud or servers.
Our aim is to determine the ideal approach for modeling and
forecasting such complex and individual/personal time-evolving
data streams collected from small IoT devices. More specifically, we
aim to satisfy the following fundamental requirements.
(R1) Real-time/lightweight computing. For real-world appli-
cations in for example, medical, healthcare, and industrial fields,
real-time data analysis is critical [51]. The algorithm should re-
spond immediately to sudden issues (e.g., heart attacks, seizures or
equipment failures) on edge devices to prevent serious accidents.
There is also a demand for smaller devices, for which power-saving
data processing and computational cost reduction are essential [53].
(R2) Closed data processing. The protection of confidential and
personal information through on-device data processing is also a
crucial element [3]. The ideal solution would be one that allows the
collection and modeling of individual/personal IoT data entirely in a
closed manner within compact edge devices, ensuring that original
(personal) raw data is analyzed safely without being shared with
external sources.
(R3) Individual/non-stationary data modeling. Personal IoT
data typically exhibits high variability among individual users, as
well as non-stationarity due to dynamic temporal changes; we refer
to such data as “dynamic time-evolving data streams”. For example,
as seen in Figure 1, the original data streams (e.g., motion sensors)
consist of multiple distinct time-series patterns (e.g., walking and
running), which evolve over time, in response to various kinds of
external factors. We refer to such distinct time-series patterns as

“regimes”. Moreover, these dynamic patterns/regimes are highly
individualized; that is, they tend to show clear variations depending
on the user or environment. Most importantly, in practice, these dy-
namic patterns (i.e., regimes) are unknown in advance; that is, new
patterns are continuously generated. Thus, the algorithm needs to
recognize them as new regimes, automatically and quickly, and up-
date model parameters to enable real-time predictions, adaptively.
Consequently, the ideal approach should satisfy all three require-
ments (R1)-(R3), simultaneously; that is, it must have a real-time,
lightweight, on-device data processing and self-learning mecha-
nism, i.e., it should automatically find important dynamic time-
series patterns/regimes, adaptively estimate/update model parame-
ters and generate future predictions, on small personalized comput-
ing devices. Here, we refer to this mechanism as a “self-evolutionary
dynamic modeling framework”. In this paper, we present Micro-
Adapt [2], which meets the above requirements and enables the
real-time and adaptive modeling and forecasting of a large collec-
tion of dynamic time-evolving data streams.
In short, the problem we wish to solve is as follows:
Informal Problem 1. Given a dynamic time-evolving data stream
𝑋= {𝒙(1), . . . , 𝒙(𝑡𝑒)}, where 𝑡𝑒is the latest time point, (a) Find dis-
tinct dynamic time-series patterns (i.e., regimes), (b) Estimate the
model parameters of these patterns/regimes, and (c) Forecast 𝑙𝐹-
steps-ahead future values, i.e., ˆ𝑋𝐹= { ˆ𝒙(𝑡𝑒+𝑙𝐹), · · · , ˆ𝒙(𝑡𝑒+𝑙𝐹+𝑙𝑃)},
incrementally, quickly and with low computation costs.
As we describe in section 3, our proposed method, MicroAdapt,
is inspired by the concept of an evolutionary adaptation mecha-
nism of microorganisms, which enables the adaptive, any-time,
lightweight model estimation and summarization of dynamic time-
evolving data streams.

Contributions. In this paper, we focus on an important problem,
namely, the evolutionary dynamic modeling and forecasting of
time-evolving data streams, and present MicroAdapt [2], which
has the following desirable properties:
• Adaptivity: it monitors a large collection of dynamic time-
evolving data streams, identifies the important patterns (i.e.,
regimes), estimates/updates model parameters, and provides
high-accuracy forecasting with real data.
• Any-time processing: it provides an immediate response,
requiring constant time (i.e., 𝑂(1)) for modeling and fore-
casting data streams, at any point in time.
• Lightweight computing: thanks to the scalable algorithms
proposed in section 3, the computation time is up to six
orders of magnitude faster than its competitors; it can also
run on lightweight local edge computing devices, including
Raspberry Pi (please see Figure 5 for more details).

Related Work
Time-series data analysis is an important topic that has attracted
huge interest in countless fields such as IoT/sensor network moni-
toring [12, 22], medical analysis [10, 20], social activity mining [36],
and more [46]. Many recent studies have focused on various tasks
related to time-series data analysis, including indexing [31], anom-
aly detection [6, 48], missing value imputation [28, 41], and data
cleaning [21, 50]. As regards time-series modeling and forecasting,
traditional time-series models are typically based on linear equa-
tions, such as autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA),
linear dynamical systems (LDS), Kalman filters (KF) and their varia-
tions including TBATS [32], and PLiF [27]. Similarly, the switching
state space model, and the switching Kalman filter (SKF) model
[4, 39] are designed as a combination of the hidden Markov model
with a set of linear dynamical systems. In addition, dynamical sys-
tems and differential equations are widely used in a variety of areas,
such as epidemiology, biology, physics, and economics [37, 40, 44].
Recent studies have focused on non-linear time-series analysis with
the aim of understanding the dynamics of IoT data streams and
social media [18, 34, 43]. The topic of data stream mining has also
attracted increasing attention [38, 54], including real-time forecast-
ing [35] and causality analysis [11]. However, these methods do
not focus on modeling under limited resources or on edge devices.
Gradient boosting-based forecasting methods are also widely
used, including XGBoost [9], LightGBM [24], and CatBoost [45].

Note that these methods are fundamentally unsuitable for our set-
ting; they all assume a static/stationary condition, where the under-
lying latent data dynamics do not change over time, and are thus
incapable of modeling dynamic time-evolving data streams that
vary dynamically according to various situations or environments.
Deep learning has become one of the most popular method-
ologies for time-series data analysis and forecasting tasks [7, 29].
With respect to multivariate time series forecasting, numerous
deep-learning models have been proposed, including deepAR [16],
NBEATS [42], NHiTS [5], TFT [30], and TSMixer [8]. Recently, con-
tinual learning approaches [13] and zero-shot forecasting methods
have also been proposed (e.g., Lag-Llama [15] and timeGPT [19]).
However, all of these deep-learning variants need prohibitively high
computational resources, particularly during the training phase,
which requires the use of high-performance computing machines
with powerful GPUs. In addition, most of these approaches require
sensitive parameter tuning. Most importantly, these methods focus
on achieving high-accuracy predictions using large amounts of
pre-collected/static training data, while they are not designed for
dynamic model adaptation on edge devices, which makes it difficult
to forecast non-stationary time-series patterns in real time.
In the context of edge computing and its related applications,
various studies have been conducted, including efficient query pro-
cessing in sensor networks [33], the use of edge devices for machine
learning [49], spatio-temporal data monitoring [25], collaborative
learning [26], and federated learning [17, 52]. However, these edge
computing methods fundamentally assume cloud-edge collabora-
tive learning, and do not focus on on-device data modeling.
Consequently, none of the existing methods focuses specifically
on the adaptive modeling and forecasting of dynamic time-evolving
data streams that meet the requirements ((R1)-(R3)), as mentioned
in the introduction.
3
Proposed method
In this section, we present our proposed method, namely, Micro-
Adapt, which satisfies all three requirements discussed in the in-
troduction, i.e., (R1) Real-time/lightweight computing, (R2) Closed
data processing, and (R3) Individual/non-stationary data modeling.
Our proposed method is inspired by the concept of evolutionary
adaptation and the natural selection mechanism of microorgan-
isms, which enables real-time, lightweight model estimation and
the forecasting of dynamic time-evolving data streams.
Overview. We now introduce our proposed method, namely Micro-
Adapt, which consists of the following main algorithms:
(I) DynamicDataCollection: Given a data stream 𝑋= {𝒙(1),
. . . , 𝒙(𝑡𝑒)}, it monitors the current window 𝑋𝐶= 𝑋[𝑡𝑠: 𝑡𝑒],
and decomposes 𝑋𝐶into a multi-scale hierarchical time-
series window set X𝐶= [𝑋𝐶1, · · · ,𝑋𝐶𝐻].
(II) ModelUnitAdaptation: Given a current window set X𝐶,
it updates a model parameter set 𝚯. It also finds a represen-
tative/regime model set 𝚯𝑅⊂𝚯.
(III) ModelUnitSearch: Given a current window set X𝐶and
a model parameter set 𝚯, it searches for optimal models
stored in 𝚯and identifies the current regime assignment
𝒑𝐶∈R𝑅. It also predicts 𝑙𝐹-steps-ahead future values, i.e.,
ˆ𝑋𝐹= ˆ𝑋[𝑡𝑓: 𝑡𝑝].

data stream 𝑋and monitor the current time-evolving patterns

patterns contained in a data stream 𝑋? Most importantly, we need

propose a new modeling framework and its efficient algorithm,
namely, ModelUnitAdaptation, which is inspired by the concept

complex model structure and train a large number of parameters us-

decomposes the data stream 𝑋into a unified collection of simple,
lightweight dynamical equations, and estimates/updates the param-

Conclusions
In this paper, we focused on the problem of the evolutionary dy-
namic modeling and forecasting of time-evolving data streams, and
presented MicroAdapt, which exhibits all the desirable properties
that we listed in the introduction:
• Adaptivity: it incrementally and quickly captures complex
time-evolving patterns in non-stationary data streams, iden-
tifies distinct regimes, and provides high-accuracy forecast-
ing with real data.
• Any-time processing: it requires constant time (i.e., 𝑂(1))
for incremental model estimation, and provides an immedi-
ate response at any time.
• Lightweight computing: it does not require high-specification
computing machines or GPUs, and can run on lightweight
local edge computing devices, including Raspberry Pi.

Abstract: Recently, we have been inundated with dynamic, time-evolving activity data streams generated by various individual IoT/sensor de- vices (e.g., healthcare devices and factory equipment). What would be the ideal mechanism for adaptively summarizing and modeling individual and local activities directly on small IoT devices with lim- ited computing resources? In this paper, we present MicroAdapt, which comprises scalable and effective algorithms for modeling and forecasting time-evolving data streams. Our proposed method has the following advantages: (a) Adaptivity: it continuously mon- itors the latest time-series patterns in data streams, recognizes any sudden changes, updates model parameters, and enables real- time, long-range forecasting; (b) Any-time processing: it operates on a large collection of data streams, requiring a constant time (i.e., 𝑂(1)) for model updates and future predictions, at any point in time; (c) Lightweight computing: it does not require high-performance computing machines equipped with powerful GPUs, such as those used in deep learning, and can run on lightweight computers or even “edge” computing devices, such as Raspberry Pi. Intuitively, our method is inspired by the concept of an evolutionary adapta- tion mechanism of microorganisms, and thus it enables adaptive, any-time, lightweight model estimation and summarization of non- stationary data streams whose time-series patterns are constantly changing over time. We conduct extensive experiments on real datasets and demonstrate that MicroAdapt effectively captures im- portant time-series patterns in the data streams, makes long-range forecasts, and consistently outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods (e.g., TSMixer) as regards accuracy and execution speed. MicroAdapt improves accuracy by about 60% for MSE and 30% for MAE, while reducing computation time by up to six orders of magnitude (more than 100,000 times). We also applied our ana- lytics to experiments implemented on Raspberry Pi with real IoT data streams, thus demonstrating the practicality and effectiveness of our approach.
